recipes.title: Rosemary Sourdough Focaccia
recipes.author: Recipe Mom
recipes.desc: An open, olive-oil-crisped slab with a long cold ferment and no kneading.
recipes.lede: This is the loaf that made me stop buying bread. The dough is stirred together with a spoon, folded four times over two hours and then left in the fridge overnight, which is where all the flavour actually comes from. What comes out is a shatter-crisp bottom, a custardy middle and a top full of dimples holding pools of green olive oil.

steps.title: Mix the dough
steps.text: Whisk the starter, water and honey in a large bowl until the starter dissolves and the water looks cloudy. Add the flour and salt and stir with a sturdy spoon until no dry flour remains - it will be a shaggy, sticky mass. Cover and rest 30 minutes.

steps.title: Fold four times
steps.text: With a wet hand, reach under one side of the dough, stretch it up and fold it over the center; rotate the bowl and repeat three more times. Do this whole set every 30 minutes for 2 hours. By the last set the dough should feel smooth, elastic and noticeably puffed.

steps.title: Cold ferment
steps.text: Cover tightly and refrigerate 12 to 16 hours. The dough should rise by roughly half and be dotted with bubbles across the surface when you pull it out - this slow cold stretch is where the sour, wheaty flavour develops.

steps.title: Pan and warm up
steps.text: Pour 3 tablespoons of the olive oil into a 13-by-9-inch metal pan and tilt to coat. Scrape in the dough, turn it once to oil both sides, and let it sit at room temperature 2 to 3 hours until it relaxes to fill most of the pan and jiggles like set custard.

steps.title: Dimple and top
steps.text: Heat the oven to 450F/230C. Oil your fingertips and press straight down through the dough to the pan bottom all over, making deep dimples. Drizzle with the remaining oil, then scatter the rosemary, garlic, flaky salt and pepper.

steps.title: Bake hot
steps.text: Bake 22 to 28 minutes, until the top is deep golden brown, the edges have pulled from the pan and shrunk slightly, and the underside is crisp when you lift a corner with a spatula.

steps.title: Slide out immediately
steps.text: Slide the focaccia straight onto a wire rack the moment it leaves the oven. Leaving it in the hot pan steams that crisp bottom soft within minutes. Cool 15 minutes before cutting.

tips: Your starter must be at its peak - domed and bubbly, not collapsed. A sluggish starter gives a dense, flat slab no amount of extra time will fix.
Metal pan, not glass. Glass insulates and you will never get the fried, crisp underside that makes this worth doing.
Leftovers split horizontally and grilled make the best sandwich bread in this house.
recipes.cooksNote: The half cup of olive oil looks alarming and it is not a mistake. The oil in the pan effectively shallow-fries the base while the top bakes, and that contrast between crackling bottom and open, tender crumb is the entire point of pan focaccia. Use oil you would happily taste on a salad, because you will absolutely taste it here.

recipes.title: Hyderabadi Chicken Biryani
recipes.author: Mom
recipes.desc: Yogurt-marinated chicken layered under saffron basmati and steamed sealed until every grain is separate.
recipes.lede: Biryani is a project and I will not pretend otherwise, but it is the kind of project that makes a table go quiet. The chicken marinates in spiced yogurt, the rice is parboiled to exactly seventy percent, and then the two steam together under a sealed lid so the meat perfumes the grain. Get the rice timing right and everything else follows.

items.name: bone-in chicken thighs
items.note: skin removed, slashed to the bone

items.name: saffron threads
items.note: a generous pinch, steeped in the warm milk

steps.title: Marinate the chicken
steps.text: Whisk the yogurt with the ginger-garlic paste, chile powder, turmeric, garam masala, and a heavy pinch of salt, then turn the chicken through it until every slash is coated. Leave at least 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.

steps.title: Fry the onions
steps.text: Heat the ghee in a heavy pot and fry the sliced onions over medium heat for 15 to 18 minutes, stirring often, until they are a deep even brown and crisp at the edges. Lift half out onto paper towel — those are your garnish.

steps.title: Parboil the rice
steps.text: Boil a large pot of well-salted water and cook the drained rice for 5 to 6 minutes only. It is ready when a grain snaps cleanly between your fingers but still has a hard white core — about seventy percent done. Drain immediately.

steps.title: Cook the chicken down
steps.text: Add the marinated chicken and all its yogurt to the pot with the remaining onions and cook uncovered over medium heat for 12 to 15 minutes, until the sauce thickens and pools of ghee separate at the edges.

steps.title: Layer it up
steps.text: Spread the rice evenly over the chicken without stirring. Scatter the mint, cilantro, and reserved fried onions on top, then drizzle the saffron milk across the surface in stripes so the finished rice is mottled orange and white.

steps.title: Seal and steam
steps.text: Cover with a tight lid, wrapping the rim in foil or a damp towel if it does not seal well. Cook on the lowest heat for 25 minutes, then rest off the heat 10 minutes more. The rice is done when the top grains are fully tender and steam rushes out as you lift the lid.

steps.title: Serve from the bottom up
steps.text: Dig straight down to the base with a wide spoon and lift, bringing chicken and sauce up through the rice rather than stirring it in. Serve with cool yogurt raita.

tips: Aged basmati is worth hunting down — it absorbs less water and stays separate under the steam.
Fry the onions further than feels comfortable. Pale onions taste of nothing here.
A heat diffuser or an empty skillet under the pot stops the bottom layer scorching.
Leftovers reheat beautifully with a splash of water and a covered pan.
recipes.cooksNote: The parboil is the whole recipe in one step. Rice that goes into the pot fully cooked turns to paste under twenty-five minutes of steam, and rice pulled too early stays chalky at the core because there is not enough liquid left in the pot to save it. Start testing grains at four minutes and pull the pot the moment the snap goes from brittle to just-yielding.

recipes.title: Ginger Scallion Shrimp Fried Rice
recipes.author: Mom
recipes.desc: Cold leftover rice fried hard with shrimp, egg, and a heavy hand of ginger. Twenty minutes, one pan.
recipes.lede: Fried rice is the recipe that punishes you for being organised — it needs day-old rice, dried out and cold from the fridge, so the grains stay separate instead of steaming into mush. Everything else is speed. Have every ingredient chopped and sitting by the stove before the pan gets hot, because once it starts there is no time to go looking for the soy sauce.

steps.title: Set up first
steps.text: Break the cold rice apart with wet hands until there are no clumps, and line up every other ingredient in bowls next to the stove. The cooking takes eight minutes and there is no pausing once you start.

steps.title: Scramble the eggs
steps.text: Heat 1 tablespoon of oil in a wok or large skillet over high until it just smokes, pour in the beaten eggs, and scramble for about 45 seconds until barely set and still glossy. Tip them out onto a plate.

steps.title: Sear the shrimp
steps.text: Add another tablespoon of oil and spread the shrimp in a single layer. Cook 1 to 2 minutes per side, until they curl loosely into a C shape and turn opaque with pink edges, then move them out with the eggs. A tight O means overcooked.

steps.title: Fry the aromatics
steps.text: Add the last of the oil with the ginger, garlic, and scallion whites and stir constantly for 30 seconds — just until fragrant and sizzling, before the garlic takes any colour. Toss in the frozen peas and carrots for a minute.

steps.title: Fry the rice hard
steps.text: Add the rice and press it against the pan, letting it sit 30 seconds between tosses. Keep going for 4 to 5 minutes until the grains are separate, hot through, and you hear them popping against the metal.

steps.title: Bring it back together
steps.text: Drizzle the soy and oyster sauce down the side of the pan so they hit hot metal and caramelise, then fold in the eggs, shrimp, and scallion greens. Off the heat, add the sesame oil and white pepper, taste, and serve immediately.

tips: No day-old rice? Spread fresh rice on a sheet pan and freeze it uncovered for 30 minutes.
Cook in two batches if your pan is small. Crowded rice steams and never crisps.
Sauce down the hot side of the pan, never straight onto the rice — that is where the smoky flavour comes from.
recipes.cooksNote: Your burner is almost certainly weaker than a restaurant wok range, so the fix is to stop treating it like a stir-fry and let the rice sit still. Pressing a layer flat and leaving it undisturbed for thirty seconds at a time builds far more browning than constant tossing does on a home stove. Loud and a little scary is the correct sound.

recipes.title: Blistered Basil Drunken Noodles
recipes.author: Mom
recipes.desc: Wide rice noodles charred in a hot wok with pork, chilies and a fistful of holy basil.
recipes.lede: This is the noodle dish I make when the day has been long and I want dinner to taste like it came from a street cart. The whole thing lives or dies on heat, so get the pan hotter than feels reasonable and don't crowd it. Everything else is stirring, and it's over in twelve minutes.

items.name: palm sugar or light brown sugar
Thai holy basil leaves, loosely packed
items.note: Italian basil works in a pinch

steps.title: Loosen the noodles
steps.text: If the fresh noodles came refrigerated and welded into a block, microwave them in 30-second bursts until they are warm and slack, then peel the ribbons apart with your fingers. They should bend without cracking; a noodle that snaps will shatter in the wok.

steps.title: Stir the sauce
steps.text: Whisk the oyster sauce, soy sauce, fish sauce, dark soy and sugar in a small bowl until the sugar has dissolved completely and no grit is left at the bottom. Set it right next to the stove, because once you start cooking there is no time to go looking for it.

steps.title: Prep everything within arm's reach
steps.text: Line up the garlic, chilies, pork, Chinese broccoli stems, leaves and basil in the order you will add them. This dish moves faster than you can chop, so mise en place is not optional here.

steps.title: Get the wok smoking
steps.text: Heat the oil in a wok or the widest skillet you own over the highest heat until it shimmers and a drop of water flicked in vanishes instantly. Add the garlic and chilies and stir for about 15 seconds, just until the garlic turns pale gold and smells sharp.

steps.title: Brown the pork
steps.text: Add the pork and press it flat against the pan, letting it sit undisturbed for a full minute before breaking it up. Cook until the pork is browned in spots and no longer pink, about 2 minutes total, then add the Chinese broccoli stems and toss for another minute until they turn bright green.

steps.title: Char the noodles
steps.text: Add the noodles and the sauce and toss with a spatula, scraping from the bottom, for 2 to 3 minutes. You want some ribbons to blister and darken where they touch the metal, which is the whole point of the dish, so resist the urge to stir constantly.

steps.title: Finish with basil
steps.text: Kill the heat, throw in the Chinese broccoli leaves and all the basil, and fold twice. The basil should wilt from residual heat alone and still look green. Serve immediately with lime wedges, straight from the pan.

tips: Fresh noodles are worth hunting down, but dried wide rice noodles work: soak them in hot tap water for 30 minutes until pliable, never boil them.
If your stove is weak, cook this in two batches. A crowded wok steams the noodles and you lose the char entirely.
Holy basil has a peppery, almost clove-like edge. Thai sweet basil is the next best thing; Italian basil is a distant but acceptable third.
recipes.cooksNote: The name comes from the idea that this is what you want at the end of a long night, and honestly, that tracks. Four chilies makes it genuinely hot. Two makes it a dish everyone at the table will eat, and there is no shame in that; I usually cook it mild and put a dish of sliced chilies in fish sauce on the table so people can escalate on their own terms.

recipes.title: Weeknight Tamarind Pad Thai
recipes.author: Mom
recipes.desc: Properly sour, properly sweet, and nothing like the ketchup-red version you get at the mall.
recipes.lede: Real pad thai is sour first, sweet second, and salty underneath, and once you taste that balance you cannot go back to the orange stuff. The only ingredient you may have to order is tamarind concentrate, and one jar will last you a year of these. Soak the noodles while you chop and the cooking is over in fifteen minutes.

items.name: tamarind concentrate
items.note: the dark, sour paste, not sweetened syrup

items.name: palm sugar, chopped, or light brown sugar
bean sprouts
items.note: half for the pan, half raw on top

steps.title: Soak the noodles
steps.text: Cover the dried noodles with warm tap water and leave them for 25 to 30 minutes while you prep everything else. They are ready when a strand bends into a full circle without breaking but still feels chalky and firm in the middle; they finish cooking in the pan.

steps.title: Build the sauce
steps.text: Warm the tamarind, fish sauce and palm sugar in a small saucepan over low heat, stirring until the sugar melts and the mixture is smooth and glossy, about 2 minutes. Taste it: it should be aggressively sour and salty, because it will be spread across a pound of noodles.

steps.title: Crisp the tofu
steps.text: Heat 2 tablespoons of the oil in a large skillet or wok over medium-high heat and fry the tofu, undisturbed, until the undersides are deep gold, about 3 minutes, then turn and repeat. Scoop it onto a plate and leave the oil behind.

steps.title: Cook the shrimp and aromatics
steps.text: Add the last tablespoon of oil, then the garlic and shallot, and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the shrimp in a single layer and cook until they curl into loose C-shapes and turn opaque, about 2 minutes, then push everything to one side of the pan.

steps.title: Scramble the eggs
steps.text: Crack the eggs into the empty side of the pan, break the yolks, and let them set for about 30 seconds before scrambling them into soft curds. Do not fully cook them; they should still look slightly wet when you move on.

steps.title: Toss in the noodles
steps.text: Drain the noodles well and add them with all of the sauce. Toss constantly for 2 to 3 minutes until the noodles have drunk up the sauce, turned an even mahogany brown, and gone completely tender with no chalky centre.

steps.title: Finish and serve
steps.text: Fold in the tofu, the garlic chives and half the bean sprouts and toss for 30 seconds, just until the sprouts lose their raw edge but still snap. Pile onto plates and top with the remaining raw sprouts, the peanuts and a lime wedge each.

tips: Taste the sauce before it hits the noodles. Tamarind brands vary wildly in sourness, so adjust with a little more sugar or a squeeze of lime until it makes you squint slightly.
Soak, never boil, the noodles. Boiled rice noodles turn to paste the moment they meet a hot pan.
No shrimp? Sliced chicken thigh works beautifully; give it 4 minutes instead of 2 and cook it through before the eggs go in.
recipes.cooksNote: I make this in two batches when I am cooking for more than four, because a pan packed with noodles steams instead of frying and you end up with something soft and sad. Keep the first batch warm in a low oven, wipe the pan, and go again. It takes an extra six minutes and it is the difference between a good pad thai and a great one.

recipes.title: Miso Butter Chicken Ramen
recipes.author: Mom
recipes.desc: A rich, savoury broth built in an hour, with butter melted in at the end for body.
recipes.lede: Proper ramen shops simmer bones for two days, and I respect that, but I am not doing it on a Tuesday. This version leans on chicken thighs, dried shiitake and white miso to get somewhere genuinely deep in about an hour, and a knob of butter whisked in at the end gives it the mouthfeel that usually takes all that time.

steps.title: Start the broth
steps.text: Put the stock, chicken thighs and dried shiitake in a large pot, bring it to a bare simmer, and skim off the grey foam that rises in the first five minutes. Keep it at the barest bubble for 35 minutes, until the chicken pulls away from the bone with almost no resistance.

steps.title: Boil the eggs
steps.text: While the broth simmers, lower the eggs into a small pot of boiling water and cook for exactly 7 minutes, then plunge them into ice water. Peel them once they are cold to the touch; the yolks should be set at the edge and jammy in the centre.

steps.title: Shred the chicken
steps.text: Lift the thighs and mushrooms out of the broth. When the chicken is cool enough to handle, pull the meat off in big shreds and discard the skin and bones. Slice the softened shiitake caps thinly and put both aside.

steps.title: Season the broth
steps.text: Whisk the garlic, ginger, miso, soy sauce and sesame oil into a ladleful of hot broth in a bowl until completely smooth, then stir that slurry back into the pot. Never dump miso straight into the pot or you will chase lumps around for ten minutes.

steps.title: Mount the butter
steps.text: Take the pot off direct heat and whisk in the cold butter a cube at a time until the broth turns slightly opaque and glossy and no fat is pooling on the surface. Taste and add soy sauce if it needs more salt; it should taste a shade too strong on its own.

steps.title: Cook the noodles separately
steps.text: Boil the ramen noodles in a separate pot of unsalted water according to the package, usually 90 seconds to 2 minutes, until they are springy with no raw core. Drain them well so you are not watering down the broth you just built.

steps.title: Build the bowls
steps.text: Divide the noodles among four deep bowls and ladle the hot broth over. Top each with shredded chicken, sliced shiitake, a halved egg, scallions, a piece of nori tucked against the rim, and as much chili crisp as you want. Eat immediately.

tips: Never boil the broth after the miso goes in. High heat makes miso grainy and dulls its flavour; keep it just below a simmer.
Cook the noodles in their own pot every single time. Starch from the noodles will turn your broth cloudy and gluey.
The broth keeps for four days in the fridge and freezes for three months. Freeze it before the butter goes in and mount it fresh when you reheat.
recipes.cooksNote: The butter is not a gimmick. Miso and butter share a savoury, slightly funky wavelength, and the fat emulsified into the broth gives you that clinging, lip-coating quality that a quick stock normally lacks. If you are dairy-free, a tablespoon of tahini whisked in does a surprisingly similar job.

recipes.title: Iced Matcha Oat Latte
recipes.author: Recipe Mom
recipes.desc: Cafe-grade iced matcha at home — properly sifted, whisked smooth, and sweetened with a two-minute vanilla syrup.
recipes.lede: The gritty, bitter matcha most people make at home has two fixable problems: water that is too hot and powder that was never sifted. Fix both and you get something sweet, grassy and creamy that costs about a dollar a glass instead of seven. The vanilla syrup takes two minutes and keeps for a month, so make the whole batch.

items.name: oat milk
items.note: barista style if you have it

steps.title: Make the syrup
steps.text: Bring the sugar and water to a simmer in a small pan, stirring, and cook just until the liquid turns completely clear with no grain visible on the bottom, about 2 minutes. Take it off the heat, stir in the vanilla, and cool — it keeps a month in a jar in the fridge.

steps.title: Sift the matcha
steps.text: Push the matcha through a small fine-mesh sieve into a wide bowl or mug. Matcha clumps the moment it meets moisture, and sifting is the only reliable way to avoid the little bitter pellets that sink to the bottom of a glass.

steps.title: Whisk it smooth
steps.text: Add the hot water — 175F, which is a kettle brought to a boil and then left for 3 minutes — and whisk briskly in a W motion for about 20 seconds, until the surface carries a fine even foam and there is not a speck of powder clinging to the sides.

steps.title: Build the glasses
steps.text: Fill two tall glasses with ice, divide the oat milk between them, and stir in the vanilla syrup and a tiny pinch of salt. Salt in a sweet drink sounds odd but it takes the chalky edge off oat milk.

steps.title: Pour and layer
steps.text: Pour the whisked matcha slowly over the back of a spoon into each glass. It will sit in a bright green layer over the milk for a good minute, which is the entire point of making it at home.

steps.title: Stir and taste
steps.text: Stir just before drinking and taste — matcha varies enormously by harvest, so add another teaspoon of syrup if yours is sharp. Grate over a little orange zest if you want it to taste like something you paid for.

tips: Boiling water scorches matcha and turns it bitter and flat. If you have no thermometer, boil then wait three full minutes.
Buy ceremonial grade for drinking. Culinary grade is made to stand up to sugar and flour in baking and tastes harsh on its own.
Store the tin in the fridge, sealed and away from light. Matcha fades from bright green to dull olive within weeks on a warm shelf.
recipes.cooksNote: Doubling this to make a jug for a table does not work well — whisked matcha separates within about ten minutes and the foam collapses. Whisk each round of two glasses fresh; it takes under a minute once the syrup is made.

recipes.title: Mediterranean Tuna Salad
recipes.desc: Oil-packed albacore with tomato, red onion, capers and parsley — ten minutes, no stove.
recipes.lede: This is the lunch I make when I want something that actually holds me together till dinner. The trick is good tuna packed in olive oil — that oil is the whole dressing — and letting it sit five minutes so the onion softens its bite. Pile it over greens, stuff it into an avocado, or pull it apart on toast.

items.name: wild albacore tuna in olive oil

steps.title: Flake the tuna
steps.text: Tip the tuna into a medium bowl along with its olive oil and break it into big, craggy flakes with a fork — you want texture, not paste.

steps.title: Fold in the vegetables
steps.text: Add the diced tomato, red onion, capers and parsley. Fold everything together gently so the tomato does not break down.

steps.title: Dress and season
steps.text: Pour over the red wine vinegar, season with the salt and pepper, and toss until glossy. Taste and adjust — it should be bright and a little punchy.

steps.title: Rest, then serve
steps.text: Let it sit for five minutes so the onion mellows and the flavours settle. Serve over arugula with chickpeas, avocado and a jammy egg, or spread on toasted sourdough.

tips: Buy the tuna packed in olive oil, not water — that oil is your dressing, so never drain it.
Five minutes of resting is not optional; it takes the raw edge off the onion and pulls everything together.
Doubles and triples cleanly for a batch of lunches — it actually tastes better on day two.
recipes.cooksNote: Keeps covered in the fridge for up to two days and only improves overnight. Bring it back to room temperature before serving so the olive oil loosens again.

recipes.title: High-Fiber Overnight Oats
recipes.desc: Oats, chia and avocado powder soaked overnight into a thick, green, genuinely filling jar.
recipes.lede: This is the one I stir together at night so breakfast is already done. The chia does all the work while you sleep — by morning it is thick enough to stand a spoon in, and it actually holds you until lunch instead of leaving you rummaging at ten. It goes an alarming shade of green from the avocado powder; do not let that put you off.

items.name: blueberries or strawberries, to top
items.note: optional — a small handful of blueberries, or 2 to 3 strawberries

steps.title: Combine the dry
steps.text: Tip the oats, chia seeds, avocado powder and the cinnamon and flaxseed if you are using them into a jar or container with a lid.

steps.title: Pour in the milk
steps.text: Add the milk, pouring it right over the dry ingredients so nothing stays stuck to the sides.

steps.title: Stir properly
steps.text: Stir until there are no dry pockets and no powder clinging to the bottom — chia clumps if you rush this, so go round the base of the jar a few times.

steps.title: Chill overnight
steps.text: Cover and refrigerate for at least 6 to 8 hours. The chia swells and the oats soften until the whole thing is thick and spoonable.

steps.title: Stir and top
steps.text: In the morning give it another stir to loosen it, then scatter over the berries. If it has set firmer than you like, slacken it with a splash more milk.

tips: Give it a second stir a few minutes after the first — that is when the chia starts to seize and any clumps are still easy to break up.
Build three or four jars at once on a Sunday; they keep happily for a couple of days and breakfast stops being a decision.
If you are hungry again before lunch, eat it alongside a boiled egg or a small pot of plain Greek yogurt for extra protein.
recipes.cooksNote: Designed to keep you full and your blood sugar steady through the morning — the oats bring beta-glucan, the chia and flaxseed bring omega-3, and the milk adds calcium and magnesium. Best eaten cold, straight from the fridge.

recipes.title: Garlic & Oyster Sauce Tempeh Stir-Fry
recipes.desc: Fried tempeh, snappy French beans and chickpeas in a quick garlic and oyster sauce glaze.
recipes.lede: Thirteen minutes, one pan, and the sort of dinner that makes you feel organised. The whole point is heat and speed — the beans should stay squeaky and bright, not go dull and soft, so everything gets cut and measured before the oil goes in. Tempeh and chickpeas together make it properly filling without any meat.

items.name: French beans, trimmed and cut diagonally
water
items.note: to loosen it into a sauce

steps.title: Aromatise the base
steps.text: Heat the oil in a wok or large skillet over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and sauté for about a minute, until it turns golden and smells sweet — do not let it catch or it will go bitter.

steps.title: Flash-cook the beans
steps.text: Tip in the French beans and push the heat up to medium-high. Stir-fry for 2 to 3 minutes, until they turn a vivid bright green and still squeak against the spoon.

steps.title: Add the pulses and protein
steps.text: Add the boiled chickpeas and the fried tempeh slices. Toss for a minute so everything is evenly spread through the pan and heated right through.

steps.title: Sauce and simmer
steps.text: Drizzle over the oyster sauce and soy sauce, then pour in the water. Stir-fry hard for 1 to 2 minutes, letting the liquid bubble up and coat everything — the beans should soften just slightly and stay crisp.

steps.title: Serve hot
steps.text: Take it off the heat straight away and turn it out onto a serving plate. It carries on cooking in a hot wok, so do not let it sit.

tips: Cut and measure everything before the pan gets hot. Eight minutes of cooking leaves no time to be trimming beans halfway through.
Frying the tempeh first is what gives it that firm, golden edge — straight from the packet it will steam and go soft in the sauce.
Oyster sauce is not vegetarian. Swap in a mushroom-based vegetarian oyster sauce and the dish becomes fully plant-based.
recipes.cooksNote: The beans are the thing to watch. Pull the pan off while they still have a squeak and a bright colour — a minute too long and they slump and grey out. A splash more water is fine if the sauce tightens before the beans are ready.
